story: Deep in the southern constellation of Phoenix lies a cosmic monster that breaks every rule of astrophysics. The Phoenix Cluster is a colossal galaxy cluster cranking out more than 700 new stars every single year, completely shattering normal galactic behavior. While most galaxy clusters are dormant and lazy, holding back star formation because their central supermassive black holes act as heating thermostats, Phoenix is different. Its central black hole is failing to suppress the runaway cooling of hot gas. NASA's Chandra and Hubble telescopes revealed that super-heated gas is rapidly plunging in temperature, fueling massive starburst filaments longer than the Milky Way. Recently, the James Webb Space Telescope spotted a missing link of warm gas bridging the gap. But this galactic frenzy cannot last forever; astronomers warn this unsustainable growth spurt has a strict expiration date.
angle: A colossal galaxy cluster creates over 700 stars a year because its supermassive black hole is failing to act as a normal heating thermostat.

claims.claim: The Phoenix Cluster was initially discovered in 2010 using the South Pole Telescope.
The Phoenix Cluster is located in the southern constellation of Phoenix.
The Phoenix Cluster produces more X-rays than any other known massive cluster.
The cluster creates new stars at a rate of more than 700 per year.
The Milky Way forms roughly one to two stars per year.
The central black hole fails to prevent large numbers of stars from forming.
Data from NASA's Chandra X-ray Observatory detected giant holes or cavities in the hot gas.
Optical observations with the Hubble Space Telescope revealed filaments of cooler gas where stars form.
Radio emissions from the VLA featured jets produced by the central black hole.
JWST detected intermediate-temperature cooling gas around 300,000 Kelvin bridging hot and cold gas.
The central galaxy's starburst growth spurt cannot last longer than about a hundred million years.
The central galaxy contains a supermassive black hole weighing roughly 10 billion solar masses.

disputed: Exact star formation rates vary slightly across different studies (ranging from 610 to 740+ solar masses per year); scripts should state 'over 700' or 'more than 700' stars per year to remain consistent with multiple sources.
